{"chunk_id":"dc6afe","wall_time_seconds":0.000012008,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":2787,"output":"# pg_ash: Active Session History for Postgres [![CI](https://github.com/NikolayS/pg_ash/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/NikolayS/pg_ash/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![Postgres 14-19](https://img.shields.io/badge/Postgres-14--19-336791?logo=postgresql&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/NikolayS/pg_ash) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache_2.0-blue.svg)](LICENSE) [![Pure SQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/Pure_SQL-no_C_extension-green)](https://github.com/NikolayS/pg_ash) **The spike is gone. Find what Postgres was waiting for.** pg_ash keeps sampled activity history inside Postgres. Give an agent SQL access to investigate when load rose, which waits dominated, and which statements experienced them. It is plain SQL and PL/pgSQL, not a C extension. pg_ash itself needs no `shared_preload_libraries` entry or restart. Installation permissions and statistics visibility still apply. ![A sampled lock incident, followed by recovery](assets/chart.svg) The chart shows average active sessions (AAS), grouped by wait event. Three sessions waiting throughout ten seconds contribute 30 backend-seconds. Across a 60-second window, that is 0.5 AAS. AAS measures sampled activity, not CPU utilization or query latency. ## Ask an agent, watch, or operate | Goal | Start here | |---|---| | Give an agent an incident | [Agent task](#investigate-an-incident-with-an-agent) | | See the SQL investigation | [Watch the demo](#watch-an-incident-investigation) | | Have an agent verify a change | [Agent-led before/after lab](examples/README.md#beforeafter-lock-lab) | | Investigate an existing installation | [SQL tools](#sql-tools-for-the-investigation) | | Install pg_ash | [Quick start](#quick-start) | | Configure production collection | [Scheduling](docs/REFERENCE.md#scheduling), [privileges](docs/REFERENCE.md#privileges), and [retention](docs/REFERENCE.md#retention-and-storage) | | Look up a function or limitation | [Reference](docs/REFERENCE.md) | ## Watch an incident investigation ![A completed incident investigated with pg_ash](assets/ash_demo.gif) This reel is a scripted SQL replay, not a recording of an autonomous agent. The incident has ended before this investigation starts. The demo finds its time window, ranks waits, identifies affected statements, and compares the incident with a calm baseline. The conclusion is evidence of lock contention, not identification of the blocking session. **Demo timing:** the reel uses real sampled backends with a compressed, restamped timeline. Reader output and backend counts are not edited. The [before/after lab](examples/README.md#beforeafter-lock-lab) uses real elapsed time without restamping. See [demo reproduction](demos/README.md) for the full collection method. ## Ask an agent to verify a change Give your coding agent the [lab task](examples/llm-prompt.md#task-2-verify-a-transaction-scope-change). It inspects the transaction scope, runs the disposable fixture, independently queries both saved windows, and checks equal committed work before drawing a conclusion. The fixture is deterministic; the agent must verify its evidence, not just quote its exit code. The [lock lab](examples/README.md#beforeafter-lock-lab) moves client-side work outside a transaction. Each phase commits the same four updates and records eight one-second sample calls. Actual runs on Postgres 17 and 18 produced: | Phase | Committed updates | Sampled lock-wait observations | |---|---:|---:| | Hold the transaction during client work | 4 | 24 | | Commit before client work | 4 | 0 | The lab investigates both phases after their workload connections exit. It uses separate, completed 60-second windows without rewriting timestamps. These are sampled observations from a controlled fixture, not latency or throughput measurements. Read the [captured output](examples/lock-lab-output.txt), or reproduce it yourself. ## Quick start This branch contains the `2.0-rc1` candidate. For the latest stable release, check out `v1.5` instead. Use the instructions and SQL from the same checkout. Postgres 14 or newer is required. Check out the release-candidate branch: ```bash git clone --branch release/2.0-rc1 https://github.com/NikolayS/pg_ash.git cd pg_ash ``` Install in the database that will store the history: ```bash psql -X -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -d mydb -f sql/ash-install.sql ``` Enable collection: ```sql select ash.start('1 second'); ``` **`ash.start()` does not start a background process.** With configured pg_cron, it registers collection and maintenance jobs. Without pg_cron, configure an [external scheduler](docs/REFERENCE.md#scheduling) before expecting history. Neither pg_cron nor pg_stat_statements is required for installation. Generate application activity, then inspect the history: ```sql select * from ash.periods(); select * from ash.top('wait_event'); ``` No stored observation can mean idle activity, collection failure, or expired history. Check the scheduler separately. Optional pg_stat_statements supplies current, best-effort SQL text. Query IDs come from Postgres activity statistics and require query-ID computation and sufficient statistics visibility. See [requirements](docs/REFERENCE.md#requirements) and [privileges](docs/REFERENCE.md#privileges). **Upgrading an existing installation?** Test on a disposable instance first. Keep a verified backup; SQL downgrades are not supported. Do not use `ash.uninstall()` as rollback: it deletes collected data. Follow the [upgrade procedure](docs/REFERENCE.md#upgrade-to-20-rc-1). ## Investigate an incident with an agent Give this task to an agent with a SQL tool or terminal access to `psql`. Supply the connection through your existing environment and replace the incident bounds: ```text Investigate the Postgres incident from 2026-10-21 14:00:00+00 to 2026-10-21 14:10:00+00 using pg_ash. Read examples/llm-prompt.md, Task 1, and follow its evidence contract. Execute read-only queries; do not just generate a SQL checklist. Check retained history and resolution, locate the spike, then choose wait and query filters from actual results. Compare with a verified normal, equal-duration baseline. Branch or stop if the evidence is missing or too coarse. Return the queries, observed results, strongest supported finding, and the next check. Do not change this database. ``` The [full agent tasks](examples/llm-prompt.md) define the tool loop and stop conditions. pg_ash supplies evidence through SQL; it does not run the agent or call an LLM. The following SQL illustrates the tools the agent can select, not a required fixed plan. The [read-only reference script](examples/llm-investigation.sql) is a reproducible fallback, not an autonomous agent. ### SQL tools for the investigation Use one fixed window for every step. Replace these bounds with the incident time, including its time zone: ```sql \set since '2026-10-21 14:00:00+00' \set until '2026-10-21 14:10:00+00' ``` ### 1. Where did load rise? ```sql select bucket_start, aas, detail, chart from ash.chart(since => :'since', until => :'until', color => false); ``` Find the interval where activity increased. Narrow `since` and `until` to that interval before the next step. Check the returned grain and diagnostics; hour-level history cannot locate a one-minute spike. For colored terminal output, use the [psql setup](docs/REFERENCE.md#chart-rendering). ### 2. What were sessions waiting for? ```sql select key, avg_aas, peak_aas, pct from ash.top( 'wait_event', since => :'since', until => :'until', order_by => 'peak', n => 5 ); ``` `Lock:transactionid` means sessions waited for transactions to finish. `CPU*` means active with no reported wait, not measured CPU utilization. A dominant lock wait does not rule out other capacity constraints. ### 3. Which statements experienced that wait? Use the wait event returned by the previous query: ```sql \set wait_event 'Lock:transactionid' select key, query_text, avg_aas, pct from ash.top( 'query_id', since => :'since', until => :'until', wait_event => :'wait_event', order_by => 'peak', n => 5 ); ``` These are waiting statements, not necessarily blocking statements. SQL text can be NULL without a readable, unambiguous pg_stat_statements entry. The stored query IDs remain useful. Exact wait-to-query drills require retained raw history. ### 4. What changed from normal? Use the preceding, equal-duration window as a candidate baseline. Check that it represents normal activity before interpreting the comparison: ```sql select :'since'::timestamptz - (:'until'::timestamptz - :'since'::timestamptz) as baseline_since, :'since'::timestamptz as baseline_until \gset select * from ash.compare( :'baseline_since', :'baseline_until', :'since', :'until', dimension => 'wait_event', n => 5 ) \gx ``` A positive `avg_delta` means more sampled activity in the incident window. A NULL delta is not zero; check missing-history diagnostics before interpreting it. It does not prove why application latency changed. Check the effective bounds and source when comparing older history. **Next action:** inspect transaction scope and live blocking evidence, then test a specific change. The [before/after lab](examples/README.md#beforeafter-lock-lab) demonstrates that workflow. The [read-only investigation script](examples/llm-investigation.sql) selects drill bounds from actual results. ## Export evidence when the agent has no SQL access ```sql select ash.report(since => :'since', until => :'until'); ``` Give the report and [evidence contract](examples/llm-prompt.md#evidence-contract) to your chosen model. This is offline analysis, not an agentic investigation: the model cannot run follow-up queries. pg_ash makes no LLM service calls. Review SQL text before sharing it outside your environment. The [captured walkthrough](examples/README.md) shows a supported conclusion and its limits. The [report reference](docs/REFERENCE.md#machine-report) explains coverage and metric semantics. ## Know what the history cannot prove - Sampling can miss short events and cannot establish subsecond event order. - Stored activity does not identify the blocker or conflicting row values. - SQL text is current best-effort text, not an archive of historical statements. - Collection observes the primary, not reads served by physical standbys. - Missing observations do not prove that the database was idle. - Retention changes the detail available for older incidents. See [known limits](docs/REFERENCE.md#known-limits) before interpreting production results. No portable 2.0 overhead budget has been established. Measure sampler latency, WAL, storage growth, and scheduler lateness on your target workload. ## Learn more - [Reader and admin APIs](docs/REFERENCE.md#reader-api) - [Install, schedule, and operate](docs/REFERENCE.md#admin-api) - [Reproduce the demo assets](demos/README.md) - [Release process](docs/RELEASE_PROCESS.md) - [Security](SECURITY.md) - [License: Apache 2.0](LICENSE) pg_ash is part of SAMO: self-driving Postgres. "}

Replace the incident bounds and give the following task to your agent.
Use a reader role with the documented [privileges](../docs/REFERENCE.md#privileges).

```text
do not stop at writing a plan. Do not install anything, enable collection,
change configuration or data, or send evidence to another service.

Read the evidence contract below and examples/llm-investigation.sql for

Preserve stdout, NOTICE diagnostics, exact SQL, and effective bounds.

1. Inspect ash.status() and ash.aas() for the requested window. Establish

a supported wait/query finding, hypotheses separated from facts, and one
```

The [setup commands](README.md#beforeafter-lock-lab) define that instance.
The Python script is a fixed workload and evidence fixture, not an LLM agent.

```text
its lifetime. Predict an observable difference without claiming a measured
latency or throughput benefit.

captured output, or restamp observations to manufacture a pass.

and the session logs. Verify each phase committed four updates and made
eight distinct one-second sample calls, with no sampler counter increases.
Use the actual before/after bounds recorded by this run, not the published

both windows are completed, disjoint, and 60 seconds long. Missing rows
alone do not prove that the sampler ran; corroborate them with the tick log.

in each phase. Distinguish this controlled fixture from a production fix:

```

## Evidence contract

Apply this contract to both tool-driven tasks. For offline analysis, provide
it with [SQL results](llm-investigation.sql) or an `ash.report()` payload;
without tools, analyze supplied evidence only and do not claim follow-up
queries were executed. Review SQL text before sharing it outside your environment.

```text
AAS means Average Active Sessions: sampled active or waiting backends weighted
by the configured sampling interval. By default only client backends are
sampled. Parallel and background workers count individually only when
include_bg_workers is enabled.
AAS/vcpus is a load ratio, not CPU utilization. A low ratio does not rule out
lock contention or latency problems; a high ratio alone does not prove CPU
saturation. Use workload latency, throughput, CPU measurements, and scheduler
health when available. If they are absent, state what remains unknown.

Read effective window bounds, source, and bucket resolution before comparing
numbers. Preserve and interpret NOTICE diagnostics with the result. A notice
starting "pg_ash partial source:" discloses omitted newer raw observations;
describe that result as partial and do not infer complete-window load from it.
A source label or absence of this notice does not prove completeness.
Missing stored observations can mean idle activity, missed sampling,
or expired data. No sampler heartbeat is stored. data_points,
buckets_with_data, and minutes_with_data cannot prove continuous sampling.
The currently configured sampling interval weights historical observations;
a cadence change or scheduler drift can invalidate comparisons. Coarse-cadence
minute extrema are estimates: bucket boundaries can assign two tick weights
to one minute even when the active-backend count did not increase.

For an ash.report() payload:
- aas_avg, aas_worst1m, aas_p99, and aas_p999 describe the one-minute series
  over activity-bearing rollup minutes. They are not automatically full-window
  averages or percentiles when observations are missing.
- cpu means CPU*: active with no reported wait, including uninstrumented paths.
  io includes IO waits, ipc interprocess coordination, lock transaction or
  object locks, and lwlock internal lightweight locks.
- total includes only cpu, io, ipc, lock, and lwlock. Other captured classes
  are excluded. Each class has its own extreme minutes: class maxima need not
  coincide with the total peak and must not be added together.
- top_events_* describe each non-CPU class's own extreme minute or percentile
  set. top_queryids_* contain IDs, not SQL text, for raw-covered extreme
  minutes. Missing class keys and partial attribution are possible. Values in
  event(aas) and queryid(aas) entries are AAS rounded to one decimal; they need
  not match or sum to class values rounded to two decimals.
- top_queryids_available says that at least one attribution key is available;
  it is independent of pg_stat_statements and does not promise full coverage.
- coverage.from, coverage.to, and coverage.source describe the report's base
  observations. minutes_expected and minutes_with_data describe the requested
  minute grid and activity-bearing minutes. raw_retention_start is a logical
  planning boundary, not the exact physical attribution cutoff.
- vcpus, when present, is caller-supplied and only echoed. Do not invent it.
- Base metrics require rollup_1m; NULL is not a healthy, zero-load report.
  Query attribution additionally needs raw samples. Ignore unfamiliar additive
  keys unless their documented meaning is supplied.

For a five-step investigation, relate the headline load, ranked waits, selected
spike window, affected query IDs, and raw evidence. Query text from
pg_stat_statements is best-effort current text, not historical SQL stored by
pg_ash; it can be NULL even when query IDs are available. Waiting query IDs
identify affected statements, not necessarily blocking statements. These
samples do not establish conflicting row values or subsecond event ordering.

Return:
1. The observed window, average and peak load, source, and resolution.
2. The strongest supported wait/query finding, with its exact evidence.
3. A plausible explanation, clearly marked as a hypothesis if unproven.
4. One concrete next investigation step to distinguish that hypothesis.
5. Any missing observations, attribution, or workload context that limits the
   conclusion. Do not assign an automatic healthy/overloaded verdict from
   AAS/vcpus alone or prescribe application changes without their semantics.
```

# pg_ash incident investigation

## Finding

The retained activity is dominated by a compute-shaped statement in `appdb`, query ID `2642533687498376244`:

```sql
select sum(length(md5(i::text))) from generate_series($1, $2) as i
```

In the observed incident drill window **2026-10-21 22:01:00+00 through 22:03:00+00 (exclusive)**, all 30 retained backend observations are `CPU*` for this query. Each observation contains one active backend. This supports active execution with no reported wait, consistent with computation in the MD5/generate_series aggregate. It does **not** establish CPU saturation, a lock incident, measured CPU utilization, or the cause of application latency. No Lock, IO, IPC, or LWLock wait was returned for this window.

## Scope and provenance

Only the supplied SQL connection and supplied public documentation were used. Database queries were read-only; the reproducible investigation uses a repeatable-read, read-only transaction with a 30-second statement timeout and rolls back. No database state was changed.

Executed SQL is in `evidence.sql`; full stdout and NOTICE diagnostics are in `evidence.txt` in this directory. Initial discovery also executed `select * from ash.periods();`, which located activity only in three recent minutes. No incident bounds were supplied, so the investigation froze the discovered five-minute window `[2026-10-21 21:59:00+00, 2026-10-21 22:04:00+00)` and chose the two elevated minutes from returned timeline buckets.

## Load and timing evidence

The five-minute window returned source `rollup_1m`, effective bucket 1 minute, 5 expected buckets, 3 with data, 31 weighted backend-seconds, average AAS 0.10, and peak one-minute AAS 0.27. The minute timeline was:

- 21:59: no data; AAS NULL.
- 22:00: no data; AAS NULL.
- 22:01: AAS 0.27.
- 22:02: AAS 0.23.
- 22:03: AAS 0.02.

The drill window `[22:01,22:03)` returned source `raw`, effective bucket 1 minute, 2 expected / 2 activity-bearing buckets, 30 backend-seconds, average AAS 0.25, peak/p99 minute AAS 0.27. These are sample-weighted quantities, not measured query duration or instantaneous concurrency peaks.

Wait ranking returned `CPU*` alone: 100%, 30 backend-seconds. The CPU*-filtered query ranking returned only query `2642533687498376244`, with the same load. Its query-filtered wait profile also returned only CPU*.

A bounded `ash.samples(..., wait_event=>'CPU*', query_id=>2642533687498376244, n=>100)` returned all 30 matching rows, spanning **22:01:22 through 22:02:14 UTC**. All rows have database `appdb`, one active backend, and the query above. Observations are not continuous: for example there is a gap between 22:01:36 and 22:01:57. These timestamps cannot distinguish workload pauses from missed collection or identify separate executions.

The initial five-minute raw sample inspection returned 31 rows total: those 30 rows plus one CPU* observation at 22:03:57 for query `-649674272853049531`, current text `select ash.rollup_minute()`. Thus the tiny 22:03 tail is collector/rollup activity, not evidence that the application query remained active through that minute. Disappearance from samples alone does not establish application recovery.

## Baseline comparison and limits

The preceding equal-duration candidate baseline was `[2026-10-21 21:59:00+00, 2026-10-21 22:01:00+00)`. It had **zero activity-bearing buckets** and cannot be verified as normal. Although scalar `ash.aas()` displayed zeros, `ash.compare()` correctly returned NULL baseline values and NULL delta and emitted:

> ash.compare: window 1 (2026-10-21 21:59:00+00 to 2026-10-21 22:01:00+00) has no data coverage — its columns and avg_delta are NULL, not zero. Check retention with ash.status() before reading a delta as a change.

Therefore no quantitative change from a verified normal baseline is established.

`ash.status()` reported version 2.0-rc1, sampling enabled, configured interval 1 second, include_bg_workers=false, 31 raw rows, three minute-rollup rows from 22:01 through 22:03, and no hour rollups. Raw logical retention boundary was 2026-10-20 21:52 UTC; installation was 2026-10-21 21:52:45 UTC. Missed/skipped/insert-error counters were zero. These current counters and activity-bearing rows do not prove historical scheduler continuity. No sampler heartbeat is stored. No pg_cron was available; scheduling is external. No partial-source notice was emitted, but its absence does not prove completeness.

SQL text is current best-effort text, not archived historical SQL. Parameter values, execution count, per-execution elapsed time, host CPU quota/core count/utilization, application latency/throughput, and background-worker load are unknown. The apparent low AAS does not rule out latency or CPU constraints. No blocker or conflicting row can be inferred, and the observed result does not support an application change by itself.

## Hypothesis and useful next check

**Hypothesis:** CPU execution of the MD5 aggregate accounts for the observed active workload. The query shape and CPU* attribution support this, but CPU scheduling contention versus on-CPU computation remains unresolved.

**Next discriminating check:** during the same query's next occurrence, correlate its backend's per-process CPU consumption and scheduler runnable delay with host/container CPU usage and CPU quota, while recording execution latency and actual generate_series bounds. This would distinguish sustained on-CPU computation from CPU scheduling contention; pg_ash alone cannot. Separately obtain scheduler tick/heartbeat evidence and an activity-covered normal interval before claiming a baseline regression.
